title: Firm in Perfect Competition
sub: Topic 7 · lecture of 27 Oct · revenue, profit, MR = MC, shut-down and break-even point
blurb: How a price-taking firm decides how much to produce: MR = MC = P, profit or loss, when to shut down, the supply curve and the long-run break-even point.
lede: A perfectly competitive firm cannot choose its price. It only chooses how much to produce. This lecture is one rule (MR = MC) used again and again: for the optimum, for the short-run decision to keep going or shut down, for the supply curve and for the long run.
six: **Economic profit** = accounting profit − implicit (opportunity) costs. Economic profit 0 is a **normal profit**.
The **golden rule**: produce where **MR = MC**. MC > MR → produce less, MC < MR → produce more.
A perfectly competitive firm is a **price-taker**: its demand is horizontal, **d = AR = MR = P**, so the optimum is **P = MC**.
Short run: if P > AVC keep producing (the loss is smaller than FC). If P ≤ AVC **shut down**: the loss is FC. Shut-down point: **P = min AVC**.
The firm's **supply curve** is its MC curve above min AVC. The industry supply curve is the sum of the firms' MC curves (**S = ΣMC**).
Long run: free entry and exit push economic profit to 0. **Break-even point**: P = min AC, TR = TC.
must: MR = MC = P, shut-down point and break-even point
foot: Source: 3BE123 Lecture 7 slides (Firm in Perfect Competition; Revenue, Costs, Profit; Optimum of a Firm) and Seminar 6 homework, Ing. Z. Dzbánková, VŠE.

questions.q: How is economic profit calculated in the lecture?
questions.e: Eπ = AP − OC, where AP = TR − explicit costs. Economic profit also subtracts what the owner gives up (implicit costs).

questions.q: A firm makes a normal profit. What does that mean?
questions.answer: Economic profit is zero: accounting profit just covers the implicit costs
wrong: The firm makes a loss equal to its fixed costs
Economic profit is larger than accounting profit
questions.e: Normal profit = profit at the level of implicit costs. TR = TC (including opportunity costs), so economic profit = 0.

questions.q: Average revenue AR is always equal to…
wrong: total revenue divided by total cost
questions.e: AR = TR / Q = (P · Q) / Q = P. In perfect competition MR is also equal to P, but AR = P holds in every market.

questions.q: At the current output MC > MR. What should a profit-maximising firm do?
questions.h: The last unit costs more than it brings in.
questions.e: If the last unit adds more to cost (MC) than to revenue (MR), producing it lowers profit. Cut Q until MR = MC.

questions.q: What is the golden rule of profit maximisation?
questions.e: MR = MC gives the optimal output Q_E. It holds in perfect competition and in imperfect competition.

questions.q: Why is a perfectly competitive firm called a price-taker?
questions.answer: It is too small to affect the market price, so it takes the price the market sets
wrong: It always takes the highest price buyers offer
It sets its price equal to its average cost
questions.e: Many small firms sell an identical product. No single firm can change the price, so each one receives the market price.

questions.q: What does the demand curve facing one perfectly competitive firm look like?
questions.answer: Horizontal (perfectly elastic) at the market price
wrong: Downward sloping like the market demand
Upward sloping like the supply curve
questions.e: The firm can sell any quantity at the market price, so d is a horizontal line: d = AR = MR = P. The MARKET demand still slopes down.

questions.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of perfect competition?
wrong: Many small firms and many buyers
Firms can enter and leave the industry freely
Sellers and buyers are well informed
questions.e: In perfect competition the product is homogeneous (identical), like unprocessed agricultural products. Differentiation is a feature of imperfect competition.

questions.q: Where is the optimum of a perfectly competitive firm?
wrong: Where TR is at its maximum
questions.e: For a price-taker MR = P, so the golden rule MR = MC becomes P = MC.

questions.q: In perfect competition, what does the total revenue curve look like?
questions.answer: A straight line from the origin with slope P
wrong: A hill that first rises and then falls
questions.e: TR = P · Q with a constant P, so every extra unit adds the same P. The slope of TR is MR = P.

questions.q: In the short run P is below AC but above AVC. What should the firm do?
questions.h: Compare the loss with fixed costs.
questions.answer: Keep producing: the loss is smaller than its fixed costs
wrong: Shut down: any loss means it should stop
questions.e: With P > AVC, revenue covers all variable costs and part of FC. Shutting down would make the loss equal to the whole FC, which is worse.

questions.q: What is the shut-down point?
questions.answer: The point where P = AR = min AVC, so TR = VC and the loss equals FC
wrong: The point where P = min AC, so TR = TC
questions.e: At P = min AVC the firm only covers its variable costs. Producing or not, it loses FC. Below this price it shuts down (Q = 0).

questions.q: The lecture says the firm should shut down if…
questions.answer: its total revenue is below its total variable cost
wrong: its total revenue is below its total cost
questions.e: TR < VC (P < AVC): every unit produced loses money even before fixed costs. Shutting down limits the loss to FC.

questions.q: What is the short-run supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm?
questions.answer: The part of its MC curve above minimum AVC
wrong: The part of its MC curve above minimum AC
questions.e: For each price the firm produces where P = MC, as long as P ≥ min AVC. Below min AVC it supplies nothing.

questions.q: How is the industry (market) supply curve in perfect competition made?
questions.answer: By adding the firms' quantities at each price: S = ΣMC
wrong: By adding the firms' prices at each quantity
It is the MC curve of the largest firm
By averaging the firms' AC curves
questions.e: Horizontal summation: at each price, add up what every firm supplies (each firm's MC above min AVC).

questions.q: Firms in a perfectly competitive industry earn economic profit. What happens in the long run?
questions.answer: New firms enter, the price falls until economic profit is zero
wrong: Profits stay because firms are price-takers
The state sets a price ceiling
questions.e: Free entry: profit attracts new firms, market supply rises, the price falls until P = min AC (normal profit). Losses work the other way (exit).

questions.q: What is the break-even point?
questions.answer: P = AR = min AC, where TR = TC and economic profit is zero
wrong: P = min AVC, where the loss equals FC
The output where MC is at its minimum
The point where accounting profit is zero
questions.e: At the break-even point revenue equals cost, the firm earns a normal profit. Above it there is profit, below it a loss.

questions.q: A competitive firm has TR = 500 and MR = 10. How many units did it sell?
questions.h: In perfect competition AR = MR = P.
questions.e: MR = P = AR = 10. Q = TR / P = 500 / 10 = 50 (Seminar 6, homework 2).

questions.q: A profit-maximising firm loses 10,000 a year; its fixed cost is 15,000. What should it do?
questions.answer: Produce in the short run, exit the industry in the long run
wrong: Shut down now and stay in the industry
Produce in the short run and in the long run
questions.e: Loss 10,000 < FC 15,000, so it covers its variable costs: keep producing in the short run. In the long run every cost is variable, and a loss means exit (Seminar 6, homework 2).

questions.q: Why does fixed cost not matter for the short-run decision to shut down?
questions.answer: The firm pays FC whether it produces or not
wrong: FC is always zero in the short run
FC only appears in accounting profit
questions.e: FC is paid in both cases, so only revenue versus variable cost decides whether producing helps.

vocab.meaning: All the money from sales: TR = P · Q.
Revenue per unit: AR = TR / Q = P.
Extra revenue from selling one more unit: MR = ΔTR / ΔQ.
Costs actually paid out in money (accounting costs): materials, rent, wages.
Opportunity costs: what the owner gives up, e.g. a salary elsewhere or rent for their own equipment.
Accounting profit minus implicit costs. Shows if the business beats the next-best alternative.
Economic profit of zero: accounting profit just equals the implicit costs.
Produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost: MR = MC.
A firm too small to affect the price; it receives the market price.
Many small firms, identical product, free entry and exit, good information, low transaction costs.
P = min AVC: revenue only covers variable cost, the loss equals FC. Below this price the firm stops producing.
P = min AC: total revenue equals total cost, economic profit is zero (normal profit).
The firm's MC curve above minimum AVC.
The sum of all firms' quantities at each price: S = ΣMC.

facts: Economic profit equals accounting profit minus {implicit|explicit|fixed|variable} costs.
When economic profit is zero, the firm earns a {normal|accounting|maximum|negative} profit.
Average revenue is always equal to the {price|marginal cost|total cost|output}.
If MC is greater than MR, the firm should {decrease|increase|keep|double} its production.
The golden rule of profit maximisation holds in perfect and in {imperfect|no|only perfect|public} competition.
In perfect competition the product is {homogeneous|differentiated|branded|unique}.
A perfectly competitive firm faces a {horizontal|vertical|downward sloping|upward sloping} demand curve.
A perfectly competitive firm produces where price equals {marginal cost|average cost|average variable cost|marginal revenue minus cost}.
At the shut-down point price equals minimum {average variable cost|average cost|marginal revenue|fixed cost}.
At the shut-down point the loss equals the {fixed|variable|marginal|total} cost.
The supply curve of the firm is its {marginal cost|average cost|demand|total revenue} curve above minimum AVC.
At the break-even point total revenue equals total {cost|revenue|variable cost|profit}.
In the long run, economic profit in perfect competition tends to {zero|grow|infinity|double}.
